TCR12 - day 11: Wind and ice cubes
column5:
There was a busy road to follow South after Ioannina. I met a few mad dogs, but a car came in between to save me. By the early morning, I reached Arta right when the first shops opened. I had some nice croissants at a bakery and was ready to continue me path.

Like often, I had again a dip around 6 am and I did a quick powernap along the road in Menidi, in a bus stop with a view on the bay. I heard Thomas pass by. 

In Amphilochia I found a supermarket. I could however only pay in cash and was 20 cent or so short. I was already considering to put back the pear I bought, but the lady said it was fine. 

The following climb was on very rough asphalt and lead to a plateau where were many orchards, fed by canals from the surrounding lakes and rivers. After a sanitary stop I followed my route into one of the orchards, but there was no way out. I had to do a short detour to find another exit before ending up at the main channel again. 

I then checked the departure times of the ferry in Antirrio, to see which one I would aim for. My first calculations indicated 12:15 would be hard, but possible, 12:45 would be realistic and 13:15 would be too slow. I tried to aim for the 12:15 one.

I did however not take into account the crazy headwind I would soon be facing. Even keeping the average of 22km/h to reach the 12:45 ferry seemed suddenly mission impossible. Something clicked however and I rode one of the time trials of my life. The two hills towards the end and the insane headwind in the last descent did also not really help, but I made the intended ferry crossing with just a few minutes spare. I went quite deep for it.

On the ferry Thomas was already laying on a couch and waiting for me. We had a brief chat and then I closed my eyes for the short remaining time of the trip.

I had reached the Peleponnessos! Thomas immediately shot off. I however was in urgent need of water and food and I stopped in the first road side bistro to have some pastry, drinks and yoghurt. In hindsight it was not the best or cheapest spot, but at least I had eaten.

It was hot and I decided to ride along the sea, rather than following my route more through the city, where there was more traffic and traffic lights. I passed the center of Patras and continued along the sea until point where I had to turn inland to start the rough road to Olympia (the start of the Finishing Parcours). 

Right before I left the sea shore, I stopped still at a bar and asked to get my waterbladder filled with ice cubes. My plan was to place the bladder in the net in front of my chest, in order to reduce my core temperature in these insanely warm circumstances. 

Then the first of many little climbs started. The road towards Olympia was continuously going up and down and would have been even harder without my ice cooler. It worked like a charm! Every now and then I hugged the cold bag in the hot wind. I cannot imagine how much hotter it must have felt without it.

The road kept going up and down relentlessly. I found a small bar where I could replace my ice cubes and drink the cold water made by the old ones and later there was a short gravel section with a short but nice river crossing, followed by a steep climb to a village. 

It was getting closer to the evening and I had one more ice cube exchange, combined with an ice cream and a limonade. I passed many small villages were the people were enjoying some drink together in the afternoon sun. 

I arrived in Olympia in the early evening. I stopped at a random restaurant, ran by an older couple and asked if they could prepare a big spaghetti for me while I went to the supermarket a few houses further down the block. I had to stock up for the long and hard end parcours. 

I came back for the (mediocre) spaghetti, refilled my water bottles and rode through the center of Olympia and along the historical ruins to the start of the Parcours. Soon I consumed most of my shoppings, because I did not want to drag along the packages neither. 

I still passed a few villages later and in one of them I still had a drink and a sanitary stop. The hardest part of the parcours started with the climb to Kallithea. Very steep sections that lastest until you reached the village center. I switched on my light and starting riding through my last night of TCR.

The climb got steadier and easier, but I was worried that I needed some sleep, because the end of the Parcours was a long descent, which I did not want to do overly fatigued. I wasted some time considering some open places along the road until I found a bench. I planned to rest for 1.5 hours, but after half an hour I woke up because of some dust in the air (maybe wild fires?). 

I decided to continue over the top of the climb and try again lower, in between the two big climbs. The descent was quite technical, so I was happy I took the short rest. I checked the tracker app once and saw that both Robert and Thomas were still within reach and that Thomas was even resting a bit further along the road. I however did not want to push myself too far for a 7th place.

A bit further I passed Thomas, who was bivouacking next to the road and I followed his example a few kilometers further, as I intended. I slept about two hours next to the road. When I woke up the finish positions seemed final. Robert and Thomas were already further, Jonas was too far behind.

I took it easy, but kept a good tempo. The wind picked up and started to push me over the initial parts of the final climb. When the hairpins started, the wind often worked against and I had to put in quite some effort to reach the top. It became light as soon as I started to descent. I passed the broken asphalt part and reached the main road. 

At about 12 km of the finish there was the last obstacle with a 2 kilometer climb made by hairpins stacked on top of each other. It was a necessary evil. I dropped into the sleeping and seemingly empty city in the early morning. It was not at all the vibrant Kalamata that you experience in the evening. 

At the finish some people were waiting and I shook the hand of Thomas who arrived (again) right before me. My TCR12 adventure had reached its end point. I finished in 9th position, a position I would have signed for at the start (top 10), but which I felt could have maybe be a few positions better if it were not for the saddle height fiasco and horrible border crossing experience.

However, I guess it is overall a performance and result I should be proud of in my last TCR.

column3: TCR12 - day 10: That damned Greek border
column5:
I started the day with bringing the bicycle down again all three floors, with the assistence of the hotel receptionist. Then I set off on the flat part along the airport of Kukës and later I started Parcours 4 at the Albanian Eastside. There was a lot of climbing and it was not an easy parcours, but I could not see a lot of the scenery in the darkness. 

By the first daylight I reached Peshkopi and I went into a bar to have a limonade. I expected to recognize the road from here to the North-Macedonian border, but since I last past here a few years ago, a new main road was constructed, which was a lot more straightfoward and less windy than the old one.

At the border crossing I met Thomas and I asked the border police again about the opening hours of the Tre Urat border crossings. There, one guard said it closed at 8 at night. The border check itself was delayed again due to some issues. We (Thomas and me) had to wait more than 10 minutes before we could continue. In meanwhile I had TUC cookies for breakfast.

The road over Debar to Struga was fast but busy. I had decided to go around Lake Ohrid over the Eastside, because I was not in the mood for the steep gravel climb at the Westside and I already did that side in the past. It was a few kilometers longer and there were 3 short and steep climbs, but overall it well pretty smooth. Besides the border crossing back into Albania then, which was again slow because of some reason.

Now I had to get to Korçë and then to Levkovik to make it on time for the border crossing to Greece, which I was now expecting to close at 8 o'clock (but I was still not sure). The main road to Korçë was very fast, besides the climb in the beginning. In the city I stopped in the Spar for a huge resupply and a bit further in the center I still found some grilled meat with bread to take along.

Just behind Korçë I suddenly felt a call of nature. But, of course, when you need them, the gas stations had all suddenly dissappeared. It took a while before I could order a coke in one of them to disguise my other needs.

The route to Ersekë also followed for a big part a new road. There were a few brutal climbs in the baking sun, but overall it was insanely fast. I hit 83km/h at one point even. Yihaaa!!

In Ersekë there were only a few shops, so I bumped into Thomas. We left at more or less the same time and cycled in close vicinity almost the whole remaining way to CP4. 

The road between Ersekë and Levkovik must have made the biggest transformation of all over the last few years. Where I remember a road with a lot of gravel and broken asphalt, was now a perfectly smooth tarmac road ready to receive the ever increasing number of tourists. The profile was still challenging with a lot of up-meters, but the struggle was nothing compared to the nightly escapades in the gravel from a few years ago.

I reached the CP within the top 10. The team was very friendly and I sat down with them for 15 minutes to have a small diner with soup and local yoghurt. I asked the old lady of the restaurant again about the closing hours of the border and she said 10 o'clock... so now what...? 

I started the 15 kilometer descend to Tre Urat around 6 pm and I was damn hoping that the border was open. I got stuck at the same border in TCR09 for a good 8 hours and I did not fancy repeating that. 

The barrier at the Albanian side was opening, which was a good start. I however had to shout and call around before someone showed up to check my ID... did not seem a very well-protected border. I went on over the bridge to the Greek side and the story repeated itself there. Calling... no one answering... until someone showed up and check my ID. I asked him when they closed and he said at 8 pm... So that was the final answer.

I was really happy to have crossed on time into Greece and I was secretly hoping that the riders behind me would take their time at the CP and be stuck for the night. At the end, Thomas and Robert still crossed over, but the next riders gave us a very big free lead.

Now that I was in Greece I had mental issues to push on. I climbed out of the valley till I met a water source, where I booked a hotel in Ioannina and fought with the mosquitos attacking me. Further on the climb there were still supporters who took pictures. 

I then hurried to Ioannina and counted down the kilometers untill my hotel. Check-in went quite smooth. One day closer to the finish. About 490km to go. Maybe one final push?

Luckily, the hotel guard had understood me and the gate was open. I climbed up, back to the main road. The road towards Rudo and Priboj through the tunnels and along the Drina was quite uneventful. I ate the bag of cornflakes I had bought the night before and was this time waved in in a friendly way by a girl at the Serbian border. 

I had a very quick resupply in Priboj and then started the challenging climb to Nova Varoš. It is the third time I do this climb and the only reason I liked it more now, was because it was early in the morning and there was not too much traffic yet. I was however still blown off the road a few times by trucks.

Looking at the swollen mountain streams, you could see that the rain of the night before was plenty. In Nova Varoš I went to the supermarket I knew from before. It was just open and I bought a lot of stuff. I disposed all my waste in steps on the following climb to the Zlatar winter center.

Then followed the know up-and-down road towards Sjenica, but I had to stop along the roadside for a 10 minutes powernap. I made an old lady happy by stopping in her little shop and buying cookies and drinks for the road to Tutin.

I was still familiar with the long and steep climbs that followed, but is was very hard work in the heat. On the plateau I had another quick stop and when I started the descent to Tutin there was suddenly a huge traffic jam. People were queuing for road works. I sneaked along and managed to have free room for a fast descent to the city.

I did not bother to stop in Tutin this time and went straight for the Montenegrian border. I made a short video call home and had then a good resupply and toilet stop at the big 24h gas station before Rožaje. 

Fully stocked I started climbing the long col to Kosovo. I was eating my food in meanwhile and disposed the packages nicely in a bin, but it was so sad to see how many plastic packages were thrown all around in nature. Really heartbreaking. 

I had to wait at the border, because there was a technical issue with the software, but a friendly agent called me to the front, we had a chat and he let me pass first when the issues were solved 10 minutes later. The long and windy descent into Kosovo was fun, but I felt so tired that I had to take a 10 minutes powernap on a bench at the bottom of it for safeth reasons.

Pejë in afternoon rush hour was insane. It was bumper to bumper with way too many and way too big and expensive cars. I was happy when finally reaching the calmer roads to the South. There was tailwind, so the flat part to Gjakovë went superfast.

In Gjakovë I found a bakery were I sat down to eat two slices/pieces of pizza and I took some more for on the go. 

The final climb to the Kosovan border was easier than I expected. The border control itself is only one station, manned by Kosovan and Albanian police at once. It went smoothly and I asked them if they knew the opening hours of the Tre Urat border crossing with Greece (where I would have to pass the next day). They thought 24/7, but they were unsure.

After the border, there was an Albanian rollercoaster over quite good and calm roads which brought me eventually to Kukës. I did not book a hotel in advance, but when I saw a building with a sign of 'hotel', a friendly guy sitting outside told me he could give me a room. It was a nice, new hotel, but with a long staircase to the third floor. He helped me carrying my bike up, I had a shower and slept. Finally an efficient sleeping-stop!

I left the hotel and immediately found hotdogs at the first gas station. But apparently having both ketchup and mustard in one hotdog was an issue, so I took one of each. 

Soon the struggle with my right leg started again and I decided it was enough. I stopped to increase the float of my right pedal and see if it got better. It was not a full success, so after crossing the Sava into Bosnia, I stopped at the first gas station, got some resupply and got to work. 

I decided to lower my saddle and shift my cleat slightly. It took its time, but when I set off again I immediately noticed the difference. A few kilometers later I stopped for a final adjustment and I noticed that the ink of the white marker I used at home to indicate the height had run out, hence the reason why I mounted the saddle about 2-3mm too high when reassembling in Trondheim airport. What a stupid and dumb mistake that really impacted my whole first week a lot. 

After finally having the right position the pain was gone, the saddle sores were gone and I felt like reborn. I followed the main roads of Bosnia and passed all its gas stations with their plastic bags. I found a great bakery were they had delicious huge croissants filled with chocolate filling. 

When the road ban section started after Tuzla, I took the little side roads and I started to climb over some gravel sections. There were quite some small river crossings, but all in all it went very smoothly. 

Overall the part that followed was very beautiful and calm. There was a long gravel climb and a few little villages. One had an open shop where I could resupply and use a toilet. 

After Vareš the traffic got denser and the weather warmer. Between Ilijaš and Sarajevo the route was no fun. A main road with a lot of traffic and no space for me. After a final bump I dove into the center of Sarajevo and made a big order in a road-side shop. I got even smoothies, soup (cold), potatoes and rice. Those last I took with me for later when I reached the Parcours 3. 

Parcours 3 was the old bobsledge track on the Olympic Mountain border Sarajevo. To get there, you need to conquer a very steep 4 kilometer climb with sections often exceeding 20%. I took my time and walked a few of the steepest parts in the beginning. 

When I finally reached the start of the track, I first finished all the remaining rice and potatoes I had. The bobsledge track itself was fun to ride once, but you had to do it slow because there were a lot of tourists walking there too. At the end of the track there was a one meter drop, which I carefully navigated by lowering my bike first. 

The last push to the CP was still steep, but was not that hard compared to the Olympic Mountain itself. I reached the CP as 11th. So still some work had to be done in order to finish in the top 10. But with my correct saddle position I was more confident about it already. 

After the CP it took a while to reach a supermarket in Pale. The whole road was almost gravel, so I was really happy I got there. I treated myself on blueberries and continued my road to Hrenovica, where the final big climb of the day started. I wanted to reach the valley of the Drina at Goražde still today.

column3: TCR12 - day 7: Hungarian and Serbian Hell
column5:
The first aim of the day was Fiľakovo just ahead of the Hungarian border. There was an old rail track to follow first and then some little hills. Once in Hungary it was still night, which luckily meant not a lot of traffic. During the day this section is really no joke. There was one gas station open to refill, needed before navigating the Hungarian cycling paths (which were still quite good here).

I needed a power nap in Apc around 6 am, which ended when I saw Robert Müller passing by. I would still see him quite some times during the day. 

The day itself was one of the worst I ever had in an ultrarace. When the day got hotter, the wind picked up and there was a huge headwind for the rest of the day. On the open and straight roads, without cover or shade from trees the ride was very hard. Some of the obliged cycling paths were really horrible. 

I cannot say a lot more interesting about the Hungarian adventure, but I was incredibly happy I reached the end of it.

However, then the worst still had to come. I decided to shortly pass through Serbia to then sleep in Osijek in Croatia, but at the second border crossing at Batina I suddenly was taken aside by an asshole pervert Serbian border officier who went through my whole kit and did a (overly) full body search. F*ck you!

I was really pissed and frustrated and was really demotivated when I got to the hotel in Osijek. There they were also not really corporative, as they were superslow and it took ages just to be able to pay for the night. I went to bed very frustrated, hoping it will have passed the day after.

column3: TCR12 - day 6: Slovakian hills and hugs
column5:
The route from Ostrava to the Slovak border is quite uneventful. I stopped in a gas station and stocked up. When it got light I reached Slovakia and the descent was getting very cold, as there were low clouds. I had to stop at the gas station to put on additional layer.

Then there were the two longer climbs towards Dolny Kubin which were getting warm already. Between Dolny Kubin and Malatina and the start of the parcours P2b I took the steep afsphalt climb Eastwards, which then changed into a dirt road. I was hard at the beginning, but a lot more manageable than expected in hindsight. It brought me all the way to the top of the climb and after a short asphalt section I arrived at the parcours.

The parcours started in the forest with muddy dirt roads, but it was very well doable. The front pack had apparently wetter conditions and a lot of peanut butter mud, but for me it was quite smooth sailing. Then came the grass field sections and the steep long walking path down to Liptovsky Mikulaš. There were many hikers, so I had to be careful and I got of my bike sometimes for the most technical sections. No need to mess up a race by taking stupid risks.

After the city, I needed a technical break before I set off on the beautiful but long climb to Demänovská Dolina. I met 3 riders going down when I was going up, so I was not that far off in fact. I decided to first complete the parcours before going to the CP. When I passed the CP, Peta was supporting along the road and later I saw Flora in the car with Lucka and Liv. It gave me strength to fly to the top and then back down.

At the CP I hugged everyone, even if one little one was a bit moody and still sleepy :-) . Really happy to see all of them, I went back down and had a short supply at the bottom of the mountain.

I had to make sure I left the Low Tatra National Park before sunset due to safety rules, so I hurried over the climb to Heľpa. Then came the climb to Muran, where I had some more soup :-) .

Then I made a shifting mistaking transitioning to the inner ring and the chain fell off. I put it back on, but then the shifting was completely messed up after that. I did not know what was happening. When I pedaled the chain just kept on shifting between gears. Then I saw that one chain link was twisted and I managed to twist it back with my chainlink tool. It worked like a charm. Very happy to have dodged that one.

I decided to look for a hotel or AirBnB in Rimavská Sobota, which was hard to achieve. When I found one, no one confirmed, so at the end I had to call them to get in the hotel. Arriving in the city I had to find the place, which was hard, as the guy just spoke Slovak (and I crappy Czech) and the hotel was not on the location as advertised on the internet. It took a while and it was quite a slapstick, as the hotel was eventually close to a banned road which I was not allowed to use, but I could not explain that to the guy. The detour road to get there was leading through debris and bushes... so it took easily half an hour before I reached my bed. Finally...

column3: TCR12 - day 5: Home Sweet Second Home
column5:
At 3 am my race continued. After Leszno there were big roads with often cycling paths towards Wroclaw. When I arrived there in the morning, I saw three other riders, so differences were still not made since the ferry. 

Slowly it went further South and slightly uphill till I was in Paczkow, the last bigger Polish city. I crossed into Czechia Republic in early the afternoon and I had to immediately take a longer break at the first gas station in Bilý Potok, as the pain in my right leg was unbareable. 

After the stop, a drink and an ice cream and cycled into the beautiful Czech countryside towards the 2a parcours. Just after one of the first bigger climbs to get there, I stopped in Lipová-Lázně for a quick soup-stop. 

Full of energy I went to Novy Losiny to climb to the parcours start. I knew exactly what to expect of course, as I had kind of suggested the parcours to the organization. But still I am always mistaken with the length and steepness of this climb. Dlouhe Strane went however quite well and I overtook a rider just on the top. My leg was feeling better, as I was standing up cycling most of the time.

After the long wide descent we started the back side of Praděd together, but soon I was alone. I felt quite well, got through the steep gravel sections and hiked the few hardest meters of the tiles section, as I knew that was more energy-efficient. 

At the Švýcárna mountain hut I met the media team and did a short interview about the parcours. Then I went up to the top and had soup again in the hotel at the top. 

The rest of the route I knew by heart. Went down the mountain, over the bad roads and then over the main roads towards Ostrava until that was not allowed anymore. Had still a stop in Bruntal, and a hotdog in Opava, but I was happy to reach my hotel above the old pub in Koblov. There was some discussion about to be able to leave at night, but when that was settled I hit the shower and then the bed.

column3: TCR12 - day 4: What is wrong with me?
column5:
After about 6 and a half hours we arrived in Poland.we all got of the ferry, for then just to have to wait 10 minutes at a railway crossing. 

Then the real race continued again. The first kilometers went through some surprisingly hilly and foresty area. Later I reached bigger road, of which some were fantastic, but other really bad. Just broken asphalt for kilometers. 

For some reason the pain in my right leg got worse. It was an agony sometimes. I also had saddle sores, which I normally never have. Luckily the problems with my achilles tendon had gone. Nevertheless, it did not go as smoothly as I wanted. Riders I was on the ferry with overtook me after I had overtaken them and so on and so on... not the kind of racing I like and I am used to.

Towards the evening I had one last resupply after a hard but uneventful day and had to still manage about 10km through a sandy dirt road area before ending quite late at night with the bigger roads to Leszno. There I had a quite good and efficient hotel break, but for some reason, I was cooked after even not such a hard day. I suffered so hard and had pain but felt like going backwards.

column3: TCR12 - day 3: Get your ass to the ferry (part 2)
column5:
The guy of the hotel was very nice and he prepared some breakfast for me. I set off in the night and followed the major roads towards Sweden. I was not counting on reaching the night ferries, but rather the 11 am ferry. That would have cause a huge gap between me and the front pack, but there was nothing to do about that then. 

After a few kilometers I saw a surprising spectator along the road. A moose was just calmly standing next to the road during the sunrise. Quite a strange feeling. I never expected that animal in that random place.

After 2 hours of riding I started to calculate how fast I had to ride to make it to what ferry. The 11 am one was logical and easy, the 2 am one was hard but not impossible. I had to have 24km/h average over the next 400+ kilometer, including all time lost for resupplies etc. A hard, but not impossible task.

But then soon the universe started to work against me. After the Swedish border many climbs came and the weather started to turn. It got very cloudy and then it started to rain crazy hard. For about 1 hour I was soaked. There was even water inside my framebags. Reaching the night ferry suddenly seemed less realistic. 

I however kept on going and tried to be superefficient. I made a superfast and superwet pitstop in a small Swedish town and kept going. The terrain was rolling and the asphalt was not very fast. It was a struggle. 

But when the rain had gone, the weather and the wind started to turn. First there was sidewind from the left, later it turned into rearwind. It suddenly seemed all possible again.

I pushed on further and further and passed through Göteborg, Varberg (where I had sushi) and Halmstad. Once there, I knew the 2 am ferry in Trelleborg was my real aim. I might have still made the 23 pm ferry in Ystad as well, but I did not really consider that one in all honesty. I would have also been a bit more kilometers climbing. 

I reached the Kattegat and could see the bridge from Malmö to Copenhagen and the whole Malmö skyline. Nice view. I saw the many villas right at the waterfront. Must be crazy to live in one of those.

The path around Malmö consisted out of a lot of twisting cycling paths, so it took a while to pass it completely, but the last 30km to Trelleborg where then straightfoward with a little gravel still.

I arrived at the port 2 hours in advance (what a waste!) And then panicked a bit because I did not find where to enter the ferry. I passed the station and then someone told me that we will be picked up there 1 hour before departure... which was delayed for 1 hour...

I waited 2 more hours and at the end 7 other riders joined on the ferry. I was unlucky not to have a cabin to sleep in. I had late night spagheti diner on board I tried to make a bed and sleep in the dining hall with Wojciek, but we were kicked out by an unfriendly steward. So we settled for bivvying on the deck.

column3: TCR12 - day 2: Get your ass to the ferry!
column5:
When I woke up after 2.5 hours on the couch, Pawel (Piko) had just arrived at CP1. I gathered my stuff, had a last toilet visit and set off on the Flåm parcours just ahead of Pawel. It soon started to climb up and the landscape became more and more stunning. There was a steep zigzag section with dozens of hairpins. Not easy to stay on the bike, but a great feat once I was up. My elbow however hurt a lot. Like I was having a tennis elbow.

Then the Rallarvegen started. I do not have a lot to say about this, besides the fact that it is stunning. Lakes, a mountainriver,... I took it easy and enjoyed. At the end of the section I stopped at the hotel in Finse and enjoyed an (expensive) breakfast. 

Afterwards, the easy-going gravel continued still a long time along lakes until the main roads were reached. From there I went to the resupply at Geilo. 

It then got surprisingly warm in Norway. There was a tripplet of three big and hard climbs before reaching Uvdal. I then dragged along a bit, it all went less efficient than I wanted. I was trying to resupply properly, but it did not really work that well. 

In Kongsberg I finally visited a proper supermarket and had some yoghurt. It then went steep up and afterwards with headwind towards the ferry in Horten. I met Lucas Strittmatter, we had a short chat and then set off to catch the 21:45 ferry. I was quite a race, over a different parcours, but we both made it on time. Together with 8 others we were on time to take a crossing before the midnight closure. 

After the half hour crossing I checked in in my fancy hotel just accross the bay in Moss.

column3: TCR12 - day 1: Let the games begin
column5:
Trondheim, the start of my last full-focus TCR (unless I get nostalgic later on). At 20:00 I was ready with about 450 cyclists at the Torvet square in the center.

My night before was okish, even if I did not sleep anymore after 7:00. I spent the day eating and drinking, going to the check in and bike check, hanging around and talking a bit, panicking and fixing my front shifting,...

Once the race set off, I immediately jumped to the front to at least have led the race once in my career :-) . After that, on the first hill, the tempo was very high and group after group overtook me while I chose my own tempo. The issue was however that cyclists kept overtaking me. Even when it became dark shortly (we were close to, but not on the Nordic Polar circle) that kept on happening. Very frustrating a kind of demotivating. 

The nature of the 195km long starting parcours of course had something to do with that. As long as you are on the same road, you see other cyclists and those tend to fire each other up. If you try not to play that game you start to feel too slow to be there.

After about 150km we came at higher altitudes, the temperture dove towards zero and there was a freezing mist. I was wearing my long gloves the whole time already and I was quick enough to put on a warm layer, so I suffered less than many others. But it was a first indication that Norway is not to be messed around with. 

In Røros the long starting parcours finally ended. It was early morning and I must have been in 60th-70th position (or that was at least how it felt like). Lot's of work to be done! The good thing was that the field was quite stretched out by now and I was not surrounded by other cyclists the whole time anymore. I like that more. But, as there are not a lot a routing options in the part of Norway, it still felt quite busy for and ultrarace to me.

In Alvdal I had my first bigger resupply. There were already 3-4 others present there, a feeling that I am not used to. I was however efficient and left earlier than most others.

I had opted for the Southern route following the Stor-Hira to reach the town of Ringebu. It was the first time I could admire the real Norwegian beauty. A long but quite steady climb ending on a treeless peak with far views on Mountain ranges with snow.

A resupply and some stretches of Norwegian cycle paths with short encounters with other riders later, I started the Jotunheimvegen. The first parts were steep , but the gravel quite smooth. The whole beautiful off road section ended with the parcours 1a along the Vinstre lake.

The suffering was then not over yet however. To get back to civilization, you had to dig yourself out of the hole and over the crest to Beitostølen. A visit to the local Spar was more than deserved.

After that, it was a climbing fest again, but with good gravel again and in a wonderful nature landscape. It was however a struggle the whole way. I did not feel 100%. Another rider overtook me and then rushed away in the downhill. I felt like a bag of potatoes. Everything felt like cycling through glue.

It went better once I reached the main road to Lærdalsøyri and my gps climb indication was off by a lot because of the high cliffs along the road.

Then came the Erdalsvegen. It was getting dark when I started. Completely alone I hoisted myself on the long steep climb. I stopped a few times for a short break. When the trees dissappeared and the landscape opened, the views were amazing. Even in the dark the moon and star light revealed Norway's beauty. Mountain lakes, wild streams, rock formations,...

I started the descent without an additional layer and that was a mistake. Soon I had to stop and put on my gloves and jacket. Not an easy feat with frozen fingers. It did not go smoothly, so I got frustrated. I was tired. 

When I finally got down, I had to drag myself along the sea to the finish line. Even if it was less than 20km, I was still considering sleeping here and now. I was done. I eventually went on and reached CP1. Had my brevet stamped, got out my bivvy bag and slept on the couch.

column5: The condition is a drama

I slept through my alarm (or I did not set it correctly), but the cold woke me up after about 1 hour. I gathered all my stuff and continued towards the finish. I check the location of the competition and maybe I could still exchange that certain 3rd place for a 2nd one. Thomas was not that far ahead. 

Before setting off I solved my dragging front disc brake for once and for all. I took out the front wheel, pushed the brake pads sideways and reinstalled the wheel. Finally... it seems to be solved.

The first town I passed was Saint-Jean-de-Pied and there they had something which can be seen as an ultracyclist's heaven: a pizza automate next to a normal vending machine. Of course I had to stop and enjoy a great pizza and some drinks. It was amazing. Ready to go all the way to the finish line!

I continued over a few smaller hills until I met the longer one to cross the border. The first 100 meters where beyond steep, so I had to get off. But after that it was quite smooth sailing. I arrived in Navarro and put on extra clothes again for the downhill. There were a few punchy climbs to get to the valley with the city Elizondo and the beautiful Navarro villages.

Twice I stopped on a bench for a power nap. During the last one my foot was dangling over the edge and when I got up it was sleeping. The first minutes of pedal strokes were painful. I still found another vending machine with some cokes and got some more sugar supplies. 

It took a very long time, but I was approaching the finish parcours. I checked Thomas' position and he was not that far off. The parcours started with a long climb, but not that steep. I decided to put everything on everything on the hill to see how far I can get and if I can still get close to him. Full gas! Here we go! Enough of playing the careful waiting game.

On the top I continued eating my candies and put my warmer clothes on. On the downhill I got my phone on standby and saw that the gap was less than 3km. I kept on going full throttle.

Later the tracker showed that I passes Thomas, but sadly it soon showed a glitch. Is was also surprised, because I had not seen any cyclist. I however got closer while approaching the city of Hernani. It was quite madness in the city and then, when to road started to go up at the start of the final climbs, I could see his tail light...

I got really close, to about 10 meters, but then it got really steep and my legs exploded. The 50km long chase had its consequences. I tried to come back still in the city, but I made a few navigation errors and the fact that we were racing at 40kph on cycling paths in the middle of a city, did not make me feel any safer.

Again some steeper sections came and I just felt my energy drain. I had to give it up, even after a great comeback and battle. I very slowly finished the hills above San Sebastian (man they were steep) and took my time in the city center to manoeuver the morning traffic and the money traffic lights.

When I arrived 3rd, Thomas was waiting for me. It was close and maybe with all issues encountered the order could have been reversed, but kudos to him. Nevertheless, I am more than proud of my 3rd 3rd place on a big LostDot race.

Hope you enjoyed it!

I got up after a bit longer sleep than usual and ate the pasta that I bought in the supermarket and drank a liter of drink yoghurt. I had to be ready for what was coming: the Peyresourde, followed by the Aspin and the Tourmalet. It was night, so I should not count on any resupplies.

The Peyresourde went quite easy still. Because it was a full moon I could see the landscape quite well. After another cold descent followed the Aspin. I tried to eat during the climb in order to be ready for the Tourmalet.

The Tourmalet is long, but not super hard. I stopped halfway to take off my jacket and eat something, but once I approached La Mongie I was getting some difficulties. I kind of counted down the meters at the end. 

My battery light was almost out of energy, so I was happy when I reached the summit and could use my dynamo lighgs without any penalty. The descent was very long, fast and cold and only in Pierrefitte I found something ressembling a supermarket. I was a very popular place for school kids to still buy some candy. I bought chocolate puddings and ate them in a messy way.

After the descent was finished ans it was light I started the Col de Spandelles. A very strange and annoying climb which changes gradient constantly. It becomes a gravel climb with the same issue. A very difficult climb, especially mentally. I was really happy to reach the top of the climb at the Soulor and had an excellent (but overpriced) soup at the restaurant at the top.

With new fuel I followed the route down and then up a few kilometers to the top of the Aubisque. The landscape here was incredible. On the top I met de control car again and gave a short interview. My front dicsbrake was also already dragging the whole time, so I tried to solve it there for once and for all (only with partial success).

The end of the Aubisque descent brought me to Bielle, where I arrived just minutes late to be able to buy food at the local bakery. During the lunchtime the two restaurants on the little square were open however. One of them had ready-made chicken with rice.

Between Bielle and my next stop in Sarrance I went over the Marie Blanche and the Ichère, of which I mainly remember that it was so hot. In Sarrance I stopped (again) in a restaurant to have a (quick) lunch menu and many limonades and water glasses. I had to be ready for the long night already, as there was only a small chance I would still find something open.

The Col de Labays after Sarrance starts in a nice canyon but soon becomes very steep. It is a long climb that went on forever. I was really in stand-by made. On the top the control car said hello again and took some pictures.

On the long descent towards the last climb of the Raid Parcours (finally), I knew there might be a small shop in the village of La Caserne. When arriving there, I asked a man and he brought me to the very small and local shop/storage room of his parents. I bought me supplies, ate my yoghurts and chatted a bit with the friendly man. He said he was going the follow the rest of my endeavours still.

In Licq the last climb to Bostmendienta started. At the end, it was easier than I thought. By the time I reached the top I got misty however. I had to answer a nature's call and then decided to take the road option away from the parcours and start the descent. It was dark when I was at the bottom.

Now that the Raid was over, the hills were not yet. I had to go over one last mega mountain before I met flatter land on the way to the final parcours. This climb was 20km with very steep sections in the beginning. It was very remote. Just a few guest houses, but else nothing. It got really misty again towards the top and it was sometimes hard to see the animals next to or on the road. I almost hit an group of sheep on the descent.

Luckily the mist soon dissappeared when you got to lower altitudes and after a while I reached Saint-Jean-le-Vieux. As it was still to far to go all the way to the finish, I opted to eat my chips and have a one hour nap on a bench in the bus stop. It was around 23:00 and just then they switched off the lights inside the stop. Excellent timing! A short nap and then all the way to the finish line!

I woke up as agreed with the old man around 11:00 and went downstairs. His wife had made some pasta and I got cheese and saucisses offered. I got an apple and some yoghurt and almonds for on the way. I spend way longer than I should have sitting with the guy, but it was just a nice time. He only asked me to pay his 10 euros.

I set off and immediately got the col de Chouila. After that there was the Port de Lers and I reached the top of the Col d'Agnes by the time it got light. The descent was again very cold. So cold that I had to stop at the first shop/coffee bar I met in a small village. The local men came there to have their coffee before work, I came there to heat up. I had some snacks and two mugs of hot chocolate milk.

When I was feeling a little warmer I continued to Seix where there was a supermarket. I got my drinking yoghurt and supplies for the day. After that came the Col de la Core. It was getting warm. On the top of the Col de la Core we were required to follow the gravel descent. 

I was a quite eventless descent until I approached Castillon-en-Courseran. About 5km from the village a farmer was trying to catch his cow. I tried to pass by slowly, but the cow kept on running away. The farmer got really mad at me. But it was not my fault, even when I stopped the cow kept on running for kilometers, with the farmer chasing his. I stayed at a safe distance the rest of the descent.

In the town there was a shop and a bar, but for some reason I still do not understand, I skipped it. I continued towards the Portet d'Aspet and stopped once in a public toilet and once at a bar to have a coke. 

When I reached the village of Portet d'Aspet I stopped at the restaurant and asked what I could get the quickest. I got some soup, but it still took a while. 

Then came the Col de Mente and the Col d'Artigaux. It is on that gravel climb just before the Spanish border that Maxime overtook me. I was pushing quite hard, but immediately felt that he was a lot stronger. We chatted for a bit, but then I let him continue.

The descent to Melles was quite technical. At the bottom I saw Maxime still at the first gas station in Spain. I got some Russian salad and other supplies. As it was getting later in the afternoon, I was going to try to reach Bagneres-de-Luchon and sleep there. I might be a bit early and waste some daylight, but I felt I needed some longer rest. 

The only big obstacle still was the Portillon and the gravel end they glued to the climb. It felt endless. I was really happy when I could descent into France again and reach the city. Two scratched riders cheered on me and gave me a hug. I went to the supermarket twice (once for dinner and once for breakfast), found a hotel and spoke for 5 minutes with the guys of the control car. At that moment I did not really care about the race anymore. I also knew I was not first anymore. We would see were we would end up, now I needed rest.

I woke up at the Mediterrenean Sea and rode in the cold night inland towards Albanya, the CP5. It was hilly and against wind and there was nobody on the streets, besides some foxes.

I did not go through Figueras and also did not see any resupply options. In the middle of the night I arrived at Albanya, surprisingly still as first and got my card stamped. I ventilated my mechanical issue stories and shared my worries about the Raid and the difficult supplies. 

From the checkpoint I chose the longer road option to the start of the Raid. I crossed the border around 5 in the morning and despite all the gas stations and restaurants I passed there, they were all closed. I had to put all my money on a bakery in Arles, at the beginning of the parcours. That should be open from 6 in the morning, when I am there.

Thanks the lords, that was the case! I restocked on soda drinks, had a liter of milk and got some excellent pastries. Ready? Hopefully...

The first col of the parcours was the Col de Baterie (or something like that). A very long climb, but not super steep. It took me well over 1.5 hours and be the time I reached the top it was already warm and I could enjoy the great views. The downhill was on gravel.

After that I reached the valley of the Tet where some more climbs awaited. I lost count, but they came and went. Besides one artisanal bakery which sold milk, the food supplies were scarce.

In the afternoon I reached the slightly bigger town of Axat, where all the shops were closed during the siesta (in France a thing as well, apparently). Only in a bucher shop I could buy some fish cans, a block of salami and cheese, some crisps and again a liter of milk. Not exactly the best food to get you through the Pyrenees, but those were my only options then.

After Axat there is a narrow canyon and then the long and very steep Col de Garavel starts. Only towards the top it flattens out a bit. I really started to suffer here and the food I got did not really help that much. The occasional drink fountain allowed my to get more water, but besides that it was quite sad.

Towards the evening I approached the Col de Pailheres. Quite a monster. About 20km long if I remember correctly. After 5km I saw two cyclists sitting on a terrace of what looked like a closed bar. But they were having some drinks. Halleluja! Happy to have found some place I went in and and I found a chain-smoking old lady which could sell me some overpriced yoghurts and colas. I did not mind, it was heaven!

I dragged myself to the top where I met the control car. I was really almost done. Especially mentally. I could maybe still do one more climb, but then I had to stop to rest.

In the descent I saw a place that looked like a hotel and I stopped to ask a guy standing around. He said it closed (as was everything there), but that there was a chambre d'hote at the end of the next village. 

When I got there, I first did not find anything, but then I saw a small sign above a gate and I ringed the bell a few times. An older, heavily bearded man came and he let me in after I explained my story. They got me a room and asked me if I wanted to eat. I was relieved with this support and we agreed they would prepare food for me by the time I got up again a few hours later. 

I went to bed but woke up soon with a full nose. After some struggles and slept again and got up around 23:00 for my agreed breakfast :-)

As I had hoped, the rain had stopped when I got up. I had difficulties to get out of bed and it was still cold. But then it was downhill on mostly straight, wide and empty roads and I managed to get 32.5km further in the first hour.

From Sort onwards it went up. I had to stop for 10 minutes to fix some mechanical issues with my light connectors. The climbs itselves were very long, but not so steep. So, I reached Seu d'Urgell in the early morning and I did not see any living soul, besides a car with cops in them. As there were no vending machines or anything else, I had my can of sardines before heading up the steep climb to Bescaran, where parcours 4 started. 

I ate some of my last food on the asphalt climb there. In the town itself I found a water source and refilled my supplies. That should be enough. 

When I started the parcours I noticed someone was about 15 minutes behind me, as the dogs I had passed earlier started to bark again in the distance. The parcours itself was not that hard, but just very long on not the best gravel. There were any beautiful horses living on these mountians. I reached the top just after sunrise, which made the short rocky descent a bit safer. After that there was a second longer and smoother descent.

Luckily I was also informed on time that the location of CP4 had changed, so I followed the route proposed by the organizers to get there. Maybe a different option would have been a bit faster, but I did not want to bother spending the time and energy to figure that out. 

As became a habit now, I had to put on extra layers before every descent and take them off on the climb. The Pyrenees can be very cold in the valleys but still warm if the sun is shining.

After a last shorter climb I reached the alternative checkpoint in Prullans. They asked me if I knew what position I was in and if I wanted to know, but I denied. But only asking that already told me I was doing pretty well (I was in 1st position).

I left the checkpoint and luckily the village had a little shop. Not the greatest of choices, but enough to refill my stomach and my supplies. Then I continued towards the 5th parcours on the French route, which I opted above the Spanish one I had also prepared. It was a slightly bit longer, but after one additional climb just after the border it would mainly be downhill and flat.

In the border town of Puigcerda I saw to my huge surprise a bike shop which was open. It was Sunday around lunch time! I went in and the guy told me he could replace my rear tire in half hour, with a tubeless setup. A pity for the time loss, but perfect for safety and my ease of mind! I also bought a new battery rear light as a replacement for the one I lost yesterday. I meanwhile I got a sandwich and some drinks and with new (and hopefully better) rubber I set off to France and passed the Spanish exclave Livia. 

The climb into France was harder then it should have been, because the wind was blowing really hard against. On the top I stopped at a road restaurant where they had ready-made food, but even the fish with rice took them ages to heat up. I was getting quite frustrated.

Once back on the bike I decided to push it all the way to the coast. It was quite steep downhill, but the hard headwind cancelled that out quite a lot... well, as least I had to brake less. I drifted all the way to and past Prades where the route went slightly more South. In meanwhile I had passed marvellous sights. Luckily for me the wind direction there also changed a bit, giving me more side and tailwind once I reached the flatter portions. Excellent!

On Sundays many shops are closed, especially in France. But my research showed correct when I still found an open supermarket in the afternoon and could resuplly.

At the coast there were a few punchy climbs and the villages looked very charming. I wanted to push on to the parcours and finish it in daylight. As I came from the coast, I had to climb up the Col de Banyuls all the way. Especially the last two kilometers were hard with constantly +15% gradients.

One I had crawled on the hill, the gravel parcours was quite easy. It got more tricky when I had to start riding down a long zigzag gravel path. Once again at almost sea level I was preparing for a difficult gravel climb... that did not really come. The main part of the climb was in a town and even if it was steep it was a lot easier on asphalt. Only the last few kilometers were on gravel and ended right on top of the coast. 

It was just getting dark and did my final parcours descent to Cerbere in the dark. Once in Cerbere I just had to follow the asphalt coastal road for a few kilometers to finalize the 5th parcours... until my shifting cable snapped when I wanted start the climb.

Another mechanical issue...

I parked my bike against a terrace table at the beginning of the hill and got to work, a bit frustrated. I got the old wire out and stuck the new one in, but the shifter did not want to rotate. So I pulled down the rubber a bit more and removed the bottom bolt of the shifter to see its interior. There I finally saw some old pieces of the snapped cable blocking the movement. I fixed everything up and tested the shifting. It seemed to work fine on the get-go, without the need for additional tensioning. Some little luck after all.

But then hardest part even still had to come. Shifting cables are long on purpose and need to be trimmed for good usage. So I had to cut my cable without access to pliers... my pocket knife would have to be up for it. But, it is not really ready for that job... Only after 10 minutes of frantic cutting and wounding my fingers, I managed to cut through the last wire and could set off.

Even more frustrated about the additional time I lost, I cycled out towards Spain and I found an Indian restaurant where they would serve me fried rice within 5 minutes. I had to take all the food I could, because I knew that from tomorrow onwards it would even be harder to find supllies. In meanwhile I booked a hotel in the second next town.

When arriving there, the hotel was not where I had it expected to be. Dissappointed I continued, hoping to still find something further. Then I saw the name of the hotel I had booked 1 km down the road. The lady at the reception made me lose some more time, but then I could get to sleep and leave the frustrations behind. Just sad of all the lost time.

The day started early again and I set off to what was probably the first of many real climbs for the coming days. It took a while to get into my rhythm. After I passed the tunnel on the top (I love tunnels, as they often appear as punchy hills on your routing but they are fact flat), I descended to Torla to start the second gravel parcours.

It was immediately clear they meant business here. The road went step up for next few kilometers, into the double digits. Someone was bivacking on the road of the parcours. A good way to count the amount of riders to pass by and be stressed about it, not really to sleep. On some of the steeper sections my tire slept through and I had to walk for a bit. 

It was a long endeavor and by the time I reached the top, I caught up with another rider. He then promptly descended faster (in a riskier way) than me. By the bottom of the hill and at the end of the parcours the difference was however barely there. It was still dark and early morning, but you could see many tourists had come out already to enjoy the nature and climb into the nature park we just came down from. Sadly for me, I did not see that much of it.

Now that parcours 2 was done, the next aim was parcours 3. To get there you had to do a +100km road detour or opt for one of the punchy hike-a-bike options. I found some food in a gas station and sad down to eat it and then continued on big roads where the climbs do not seem noticeable from a distance (but they were certainly there). 

I turned up the long road leading up to Benasque, as I would do my hike-a-bike attempt there. At the same time I had noticed that my rear tire was already almost worn out (!), after barely 500km. I know my climbing style is demanding, but I would consider that a tire should be able to survive at least for 2000km, no? So on the way up I looked up the bike shops in Benasque and there were plenty that should be open on a Saturday before noon.

When I finally got there, I rode around the whole city (village?) more than once, but of all online promises, nothing seemed true...

So I bought lunch in a supermarket together with another rider and I continued into the mountains, still with a worn out rear tire. The climb continued still quite some kilometers until there was a plateau from where you had to continue by foot. During my route preparations, I identified multiple options for the way to parcours 3, and all of them seemed bad. There was one with a mountainbike trail over the forbidden tunnel, there was one which required you using cable to descent from the mountain... and there was the one I opted for. On paper a hike on high-mountain grass fields. First up... then down.

The reality hit pretty hard, pretty soon. First of all, the path that I had thought I saw on the satellite pictures, was barely noticeable in the beginning. It was pushing and lifting the heavy bike and equipment over large boulders and trying not to slip. After a few different trials on how to hold my bike in the best way (I even brought a rope for that), I settled on pushing it in front of me, holding the steering and letting it ride vertically on its rear wheel. It worked pretty well as long as the gradient was not too steep or the rocks were too tall. That technique however did cost my my battery rear light which was attached to the saddle bag (and which was now sometimes dragging the ground).

After half hour, I reached a more frequented zigzag path up the mountain. Things got a littler easier, but it wa still a struggle. You saw people hiking past me thinking what one earth I was doing there with a bike - especially not a mountainbike. 

I tried to keep the pace up and more on will power than anything else I reached the crest of the Pico da Pincada. From then on things would literally go down hill and be easier... oh boy, was I wrong! There were less rocks, but the path in the grass was hollowed out and I had to drag my bike down this endless slope for ages. I often used it as a support where I kind of skied down by myself. It is a miracle my bike did not break while abusing it like that. When I got back in the forest at the end of the descent, there was still an additional muddy surprise I had to conquer before I finally reached the tarmac again.

After 3.5 hours of hiking, I came out of the forest and a group of students looked at me like I was coming from another planet.

Down the hill I found a restaurant and I enjoyed a hamburger. Imagine how well that tasted! The final push to reach the parcours was a 10km long climb with an average gradient of 8%, but most of it they had packed in the first kilometers. Pretty nasty, but peanuts compared to what I had before, if you think about it.

The parcours itself was beautiful and quite easy, bit while I was riding up the final parts of the climb, it started to rain slightly. My plan was to get down again asap then and find a place to sleep before it started to rain harder. 

I reached the end before darkness set (at 8pm), but I skipped the first hotel I passed. I would pass some villages with hotels for skiers and hikers, so I was confident I would find something. When I was in those villages, it seemed that all of them were closed. I had no other option besides continuing and trying to reach the bigger city Sort, over 50km away.

Between Sort and me was still a 2000m tall pass on a big road. It all went smoothly initially and I even enjoyed the cooler breeze. But when I approached the top and it started to rain harder and harder again, I knew I had an issue. 

The downhill part could have been fast, but the poor visibility, the heavy rain, mainly nailpin turns and my lack of confidence in the grip of my rear tire made me go down slower. At the same time, going faster was just too cold.

This decent was really no fun. I was starting to get really cold and wet... until I then suddenly saw lights and a sign to a hotel 300m down from me, off route. I decide to go for it a hope for the best. The first good thing was that the hotel was open. Upon first check there was however no room free anymore (I do not think that would have been an issue, as I could have persuaded them to let me sleep somewhere in a storage room or so). A second check revealed and old room to be free on the top floor. Of course I took it. Their restaurant was also still open, so I asked for a quick soup... which took then half a hour to make and was not that good. Anyway, I had my meal and my bed, the rest was for later.

My last big ultrarace (of the year?): TPR - the Transpyrenees Race. The first gravel edition which will also go through some more unknown parts of the Pyrenees. Anyway, they will be all new for me. I never cycled or even was in the Pyrenees before. Can you imagine? I was really excited to start, even if I knew it would a hard one.

Before the race the preparation was far from ideal. Sickness the days before, a crying baby at night the weeks before and job and house struggles the months before. But life happens... I told a few months ago that I would not join, but I changed my mind in August. So here we are! According to some before the start even a race favorite. Well, you can tell what you want, I know every start line-up has a dark horse somewhere.

I started in the second last wave, 20 minutes after the first riders. That meant that at the end, everybody I overtook was well-overtaken with several minutes, unless they were of later waves.

The race start was a bit of a struggle, because of the many traffic obstacles in the beautiful city of San Sebastian. Once they were overcome, there were the known hills of the summer classic in the race parcours. I took the lead in my wave a soon started picking up riders from other waves. With wave start I however took a while before you could do your own thing. 

There was already some gravel in the start parcours and the tempo was quite high. After 1.5 hours I however isolated a could start my quiet ride for next few days. For most of the time at least. I met a few riders in Pamplona still and on the long climb to the first check point. I felt quite off and a bit sick. Probably still the consequences of the days before.

I also had my first mechanical already. Somewhere on the gravel I lost the attachment piece of my saddlebag stabilizer. So the stabilizer was still there, but basically unless and just as decoration. I decided to leave it there for now (but it would at the end stay like that the whole race).

After the first virtual checkpoint I descented towards the South and passed some special areas with elevated canals and wide open empty agricultural lands. There were some jump-overs and position changes. Something that is completely normal the first day. The first day also most of the times a day I really need to get into it. 

My route took me along Lumbier and the beautiful canyon there, highly recommanded!

In the afternoon I was a approaching the first real manned checkpoint and the first gravel parcours. By luck I for once checked my phone before I saw there was a message of the race oragnization saying the CP location changed. Luckily found out in time!

I arrived around fifth, in a bit of a grumpy and hungry mood already. It was not feeling 100% the way it should. I carried on further anyway and reached the bottom of the first parcours in Longas. Oh boy! It went up brutally on loose gravel. I managed to ride up, but there were two riders I passed who had to walk already. It was long and steep and once on the top we had to circumvent a dead cow laying on the road.

I was a beautiful scenery with big rocky cliffs and canyons. Did not expect that here. As usual, gravel parcours take a lot long then I expected and I was also very happy it was over and I did not have any other issues. My plan would be to still get as far as possible before the night and then look for a place to sleep.

And then, at the end of the parcours, when I wanted to take something out of my framebag, the zipper broke. It was beyond repair. I thought about taping it, but at the end I decided the put the stuck zipper halfway and hope it would not rain too much or that nothing of importance would jump out.

The story of the race would for me however also be one about struggles to find enough suitable food as well. I finally found a small bar still open in a little town after a good gravel shortcut, but I had to be happy with limonade, chips and icecream.

The route led up further North and I passed a gas station that was still open and had something more suitable there. Futher there was a town with a restaurant where I could still get my soup :-). When I reached Bielsas around 10 in the evening, I stopped at the first hotel I saw and went to sleep.

Little test to see where I stand and just to have some fun. I really loved it and to have that TCR feeling again. Took about 150km to get in the mood, but then it was great. Last 350 was against wind :-p .

Passed many nice towns I was never before (Prerov, Lipnik, Hranice,...). The area around Krakau was a lot busier than I remember. Going there during Friday rush hour is no joke. The roads were sometimes hard to even cross, just cars that kept on coming on too narrow roads. 

Lost lots of time going in and out of the city. But there are already some nice cycling paths. Then later I got stuck because of a car rally (which I already do not like since I was a kid) and had to find some way out. Quite stressy and time consuming.

In Poland there were so many new houses (being build). Crazy. It is nice to see people building their own house, the issue is only that they make the same mistake as in Flanders. They build houses everywhere, scattered around with no clear plan. So that causes a lot of additional traffic and messes up the beautiful country side for generations to come :-( .

The Zabka shops were fantastic however!

When it got dark, I started the climb to Slovakia, with a few surprise road surfaces. The roads around Cadca were very calm, the rain was not too bad and the climb to CZ was pretty easy. After Vsetin there were some horrible roads, which made decensing very slow and dangerous.

Had a little dip after Zlin, but pushed through and recovered pretty well to end full pass. Beautiful ride!

So now I am using Mapy.cz to navigate through the night. As you might notice, there is a little piece of the route between Jihlava and Nizkov missing here on Strava (about 25km). That is because I set the recording on 'pedestrian' for that part, which meant it is useless to upload here. 

Anyway, I slept still for about 1.5 hours in the bus stop of Vysoke with just my liner to sleep in, but it was sufficiently warm. Then great energy saving project began. As my phone would drain to fast if I let the screen on to navigate the whole time, I had to switch it off each time I knew the route for a few kilometers. Not ideal and it cost me some time, but better that than no battery at all anymore. The cold night temperatures scared me even more for a too quick battery drainage. 

In meanwhile I used my sinewave to charge my powerbank, so I had some juice for the future. That went however pretty slow and also meant that I wasted a few additional Watts with my dynamo working. 

In Moravske Trebova I visited the 24h gas station and had a well-deserved hot meal and some candy. A few more hours through the night cold and fog and I could start the last parcours. 

After it got light I had some issues to stay away and I slowed down between Zabreh and the beginning of the parcours. I wasted time with inefficient stops and resupplies. Just before the parcours start Adam crossed me on his way to the finish. I checked the race situation and saw that I could go in complete tourist mode now. I was way too far behind the leaders to still threaten them and at the same time I had enough time ahead on the numbers 4 and 5 that even big mechanical failures would not have been a big deal. 

So I started to climb... first the little hill at Nove Losiny, then Dlouhe Strana and Praded. I took the time it had to take and I walked the tiled section on Praded. In between I got a good tin of sardines. 

Before going to the checkpoint at Svycarna hut, I went all the way to the top and finished the parcours. On the way back I got the stamp around lunch time, ordered a big meal and had a half hour nap.

I very carefully and still half sleep-drunk made my way down to the valley again over the Praded gravel path and again used Mapy to avoid the main roads. When I was almost back in Nove Losiny I passed the 4th and 5th in the race and said a quick hello. As they were a complete parcours and descent behind I estimated my advantage at now at least 6 hours.

From there one I pushed hard, with only one bigger stop and the beginning of the end parcours to get to final resupply. The final parcours was relatively easy (compared to all the others) and on the final 15km downfill I was really flying. 

I arrive a little after 20h in the evening, feeling quite fresh and on the third position. I could have done better without all the mistakes and issues, but I think that at the end the 3rd place would have been the highest possible. 

Thanks for the organization! It was a great adventure!

So yes... I missed the control about 40km ago. So I basically had three options. The first one was scratching and going home. The second one continuing without the check, which meant I was not in the GC anymore. The third one meant returning on the same route, fixing the problem and reroute from there, because my original plan was to continue form Dreisessel through Austria (a climb I did not want to repeat).

Very demotivated I retraced my steps up to Knizeci Plane. It cost me about 1 hour to get to Strazny and from there an additional 1.5 hour detour to get to the checkpoint and back (agreed, I had a quick soup there). I was not happy about it, but what could I do. In the late morning I could finally leave the 3rd parcours and head towards Praded. Strangely I was still in third position, even after wasting all this precious time. 

Once off the parcours I had to use an unfinish route trial that I had saved somewhere on Komoot to get me back to where it met with the original route in Jihlava. As that route started with a huge climb, I took some time to look for alternatives still. With a little bit of creativity I managed to get past Volary without too much additional effort and while avoiding banned roads.

Once I was in the plains, the wind was in a good direction and I made more progress. Besides some final stomach issues and horrible road conditions around Hluboka, I was getting somewhere. My goal was to get to Jihlava and then assess the situation.

Around 8-9 in the evening I arrived in Jihlava and decided to continue until I was tired and then sleep in one of the  luxury bus stops they have here. But when I wanted to charge my gps and load the route from Jihlava to the 4th parcours, my Garmin went black and refused working. I ate a pizza and thought about what to do next. I was going to have to use my phone and Mapy.cz to continue...

I woke up before my alarm went off, after a little over 2 hours of sleep. That must have meant I did not race hard enough yet! 

I shoved my schnitzels and potatoes down my mouth, put on my half-wet clothes and went outside. After a chamois treatment I was ready to start. Luckily the heavy rain had stopped (for now) and I could make some steady progress through South Bohemia. I got to Nyrsko after dark, where there was an open gas station and then did the climb to Zelezna Ruda. It was a quite easy and steady climb in a nice forest, but it started to rain again. 

At the border with Germany, I avoided the banned roads and had to do some wet gravel sections. When I approached the parcours 3, there was a long climb on a main road that had been milled off for refurbishing. Way too many kilometers on a washboard. It was horrible and got even worse when the rain got harder.

By the time I reached the begin of the parcours, it was a true apocalypse. The asphalts on these roads were just not letting through water, so you got soaked from all sides. The first parcours climbs were steep and the descents were almost impossible with the heavy rain and mist. With my foggy glasses I could only see a few meters far. 

I was really praying for the rain to stop, as I was getting wetter and wetter and colder and colder. I have an excellend rain jacket, but too much is sometimes too much. When I reached the Czech border again, it got a little better, so I could warm up a bit and have some food. I went down into Sumava, following the parcours and by the morning I reached the top of Dreisessel, the end of the parcours.

... just to find out the check point was not there. I called the organizer and learnt that I had passed it already 3 hours ago. To speak about demotivating news. I am not going to go into detail on how this might have happened, or who/what is to blame, but it did happen. 

So, how to continue from here? My road takes me further through Austria and from there North-East. I do not want to retrace my steps and even less redo a big (hard) part of the parcours.

Race Through Poland, even if it more a Race Around Czechia this year. Very excited and a strong competitor's field. 

The start parcours was very hilly and hard, but I managed to stay within the top 3. When the free routing started, I went more North through some flatter part of Poland. Took it easy and was overtaken by a few riders. When I arrived in Lesna at the start of the first parcours, I did a quite resupply and started the long and hard parcours in Jizery Hory. Passed a few known places. The track was hard, so I really had to look for some resupplies. During the climbs I clawed back a few positions (including the crazy climb to the border) and arrived quite exhausted to the check point at Izerka Hala, as third rider (just ahead on the fourth).

As the queue in the restaurant was too long, I decided to continue and get to the first gas station. After the resupply I cycled through the beautiful Czech Switzerland towards Usti, where I found some soup and food to settle my stomach problems. 

Through the night I passed Teplice, Jirkov, Chomutov (and some 24h gas stations) and arrived at the start of the section parcours in Kruzne Hory. Before I went up I still had to 'settle' some issues, but after that I quickly overtook Wojtek again who just arrived after me at the starting point. The parcours was about 110km with 4000 height meters. It was brutal. I was counting down the height meters till I was there. 

2km from the Bärenstein checkpoint I still had about 200 height meters to go, so you can imagine how hard those final meters were. I arrived as second, got my card stamped and managed to get two nice garlic soups from the Czech restaurant staff working there.

I crossed the border and rode South. For some reason, it went quite difficult. Wind from the wrong direction, rain, no rain, rain,... I struggled a bit to be efficient and make the right (clothing) choices. On top of that, the route that I prepared passed a 2km stretch which I thought would be a normal gravel road. It soon appeared to be a real peanut butter dead mud track. So I tried to stay on the grass, but to no big success. Finally on the top, I had to clean my bike for a few minutes.

Quite frustrated I continued while the rain got harder. I pushed on till over the hills above Plzen, until I could finally descent to the city. There I did a resupply and tried to decide on a place to sleep (after 36 hours it was about time). My first options were unavailable, so I settled for a little hotel a bit closer. That meant I wasted some day light hours, but at that moment that was not my main concern.

The hotel staff was nice and I managed to get a soup before I went to sleep at 6 and I asked for a dinner plate to be put in front of my hotel door after the hotel restaurant closed, so I still had a big meal before setting off after my little beauty sleep.
It was still not where it has to be, but we might get there soon.
