column3: Atlas Mountain Race - Day 4: the revenge of the neck
column5:
I collected all my stuff again as good as I could and I set off again towards Ait Baha. The first part was a very difficult and vague river path, followed by a steep climb. I soon overtook Thomas Boury, but then I already felt my neck is not what it should be.  I had to stop to eat and let my neck rest. The beginning of a day full of struggle. 

I reached the sand part around 6:30 in the morning and first layed down for 30 more minutes.  I deflated my tires a bit (but apparently not be far enough) to try to cycle to through the sand, but it barely worked. Most of the 20km long stretch I had to hike. It was incredibly slow and painful. Your shoes fill up with sand and there is no space anymore for your feet. It is surprising how much sand fits in a shoe.

At the end of the section, my neck had given up completely. I would command it to stay fixed and look in a certain direction, but it would just gradually drop over time. I got rid of the sand in my shoes and dragged myself to Jerf, where I spend longer than I should in a shop eating and drinking whatever I fancied. 

Some kilometers further I decided to give it a last try and I rested for anther hour, naively hoping that that would be enough for my neck to recover. The first kilometers where indeed better again, but soon the same issue appeared. 

I got to Amskroud where I stopped yet another time. My position in the GC was already completely gone, but I still decided to see if at least I could get to the Stelvio without too many issues. It was torture to cycle on the long climb, my head only pointing down. The short off-road descents were particulary  difficult as I could not see where I was going. I could only see 5 meters in front of me.

As it started to get very unsafe and as it was just a struggle, I decided to do something I never want to do and always regret at the end: scratch. Knowing how difficult the 25km down to Agadir (on asphalt!) still were, however tell me this decision was right. I had to hold up my head with one hand or keep my head angled just to be able to see where I was going. It was not easy and it was not fun anymore. 

It was a sad ending of a great race, which went find until kilometer 900. Then the Shermer's neck popped up and it was a lost cause. I am not sure yet if I will come back, as this is a brutal race. But I still have some unfinished business and I would maybe want to prove that a top 10 is more than possible.

The Atlas Mountain Race passes (spoiler!) through the Atlas Mountains. This a very dry area without a lot of vegetation. Only in the oasis or valleys you can sometimes find lush trees and water. For the rest it is a hard life. A consequence of all that dust is that by now my nose and mouth look like trenches of World War I. That does not make things easier or more enjoyable.

I started after 3 hours of sleep at the bottom of the Old Colonial Road. Even though the road should be easy to follow, as there is a wide row of stones bordering it, I managed to again set off on the wrong foot and get lost in a riverbed. After seeing this row of wide stones a few meters above me (note that it is pitch dark here), I retraced some of my steps, crawled up and found the road. From now it should be easier.

Even though this road is pure gravel and goes up the whole way it is not that challenging. Just the two big missing parts are a bit tricky. I first went down the road and then left my bike behind to check for a path back up. Once I found the correct path, I pushed up my bike (which was easier set than done) and continued following it.

After reaching the top there is a quite long and difficult descent. Everything was going quite well until just before they end when I suddenly hit a stone just a bit too hard with my rear tire. Bang! I know there was an issue. Quickly I stopped and assessed the damage. I had a pinch flat. Tire plugs to the rescue. Because I could not see too well and I was tired, I managed to plug next to the real hole, creating an additional hole in the tire. Telling myself to stay calm I took a new plug and plugged the right hole, all while there was not so much pressure left in the tire. I used  a third plug to be sure of the sealing. 

After sealing the hole, I crossed my fingers and inflated the tire back as fast as I could. Did it work? I did not feel 100% confident, but at first sight it looked fine. In continued the road until I reached the end of the gravel section and checked my tire pressure again on the asphalt. It seems my amateur plugging did its job.

After the paved road in Issafen, the route continues to a canyon where you have to follow a slow path inside a riverbed. At the end of the riverbed there are some steep climbs to hoist you back on the plateau. I stopped at the beginning of the canyon to eat all my leftovers and set off towards CP3.

It was very cold at the climb at the end of the canyon when the sun came back. Then there was an endless road on top of the plateau which is used for hauling. Each time a truck passed you have to recover from the new dust wave. My poor lungs. When I finally made it out, I had a resupply at Afella Ighir. 

Then followed the beautiful and fresh canyon of Ait Mansour. Shadow and water! I did not stop and pushed on to CP3, which was at the end of a long asphalt descent. I arrived around position 5. I ordered two spaghettis, had a wonderful shower and made sure I was ready for the rest of the day. 

The first part after the CP was quite easy. Later a long a steep asphalt climb followed in the heat of the sun. After another descent, another long climb followed. I found a water tap to cool myself down a bit (soaking my cap, arm and leg pieces). I found a small shop where I had some tea and one of the oranges I had taken with me from CP3.

It was in the long a steep descent on the concrete plates that followed that I noticed for the first time that my neck was starting to struggle to keep up. I tried to empty my pockets as much as I could and a bit later I even ate my other orange (which was half bad) to get rid of weight. 

It did not really get better and at the end of the descent I tried to take a rest and hope that my issue would be better after some sleep. So I again settled for some place in the sand. A local still came to me to ask me why I was sleeping there, but I told him that I was not planning to move again and I asked nicely to just let me sleep.

By the time I woke up I saw riders passing by me. Looking at the replay afterwards they are the first ones to pass me in fact. In barely lost any positions while I was sleeping, as the gap was so big. I was around position 10-15 after my sleep, while most riders still had to start their sleeping period.

The start was immediately difficult. There had to be a path somewhere, but I did not find it and I ended up walking and going over a rocky terrain for 10 minutes before I went a bit further where I knew a road was and I could join the track again a bit further. Really frustrating beginning. 

I soon passed a few of the limited amount of people that had passed me during my beauty sleep and started to climb a long road climb in the darkness. They were making a new road here, which made the surface quite pleasant to ride on. I was quite long and steep and half way the climb there was a local selling drinks and cookies (which I enjoyed).

After the cold downhill I passed Ait Saoun where I apparently caught up with a whole pack of riders that had left me behind the day before. I felt quite good and kept going on the long gravel section in a good mood, even if it was surprisingly cold. 

By the time I arrived in Taznakht it was still dark and nothing was open. So again no resupply. When I stopped by the roadside just after the town I was surprised that Robin and Lukas passed by as well. 

Now that it was light, I was hoping to still score some food in one of the villages before the section to CP2, but there was sadly nothing available. The section itself was however not too difficult and after a speedy descent I made it to CP2 in the late morning.

I ordered two tagines, had some drinks and set up a bike cleaning station to  get rid of at least some dust of the last day and a half. My chain got relubed, but it was still filthy. I took my time at the CP and some riders (like Anatole, Kevin, Driksen and Sofiane) passed me. 

After the CP2 there was a huge steep road descent into the canyon. On the section I had to stop to fix my shoe properly. Earlier that night some loose stones had cut through my boa lace. Duct tape was not a proper problem-solver, two zip ties did however a better job. Overall, loose stones cause quite some damage on ankles and legs as well, when they fly around and hit you very hard.

After this section there was a quite long road section towards Ibn Yacoub. 50 kilometers straight and slightly uphill. A quite mental game. During these 2 hours I saw the bicycle of Sofiane on top of a can going in the other direction. A broken rear derailleur meant the end of his race. 

In Ibn Yacoub I could get some cola and a friendly shop owner offered me a tea. A big part of this section follows a very wide dry river bed. In the beginning I got lost multiple times, leading to me dragging my bike several hunderds of meters across a plane full of huge rocks. After a while I luckily got more clever and I zoomed in more on my gps, causing the margin of error to shrink. It is however still a very long and frustrating ride to reach Ait Kline. 

Towards the evening I finally reached Tagmout. My plan was to sleep there inside, as I was informed there should be a hotel. After loosing half a hour and riding up and down the town, it was apparent there was nothing and I gave up. I just ordered an omelet as diner in a local shop before leaving a trying to find a bivac spot. The old guy of the shop tried to rip me off by asking 360 dihram, but I left only paying 60 (which should more than cover it).

The new plan was to ride to the start of the Old Colonial Road and sleep there. I found a sandy patch and slept there. Again you had to be careful for the spiky plants there are everywhere here and want to murder your inflatable mat. Some yoghurts for diner and breakfast should help me over the Old Colonial Road.

Even tough the preparation was far from perfect, with a new bicycle, horrible training weather and a front fork I could not lock-out, I was as ready as I could for the race.  As it was my first proper ultra mountainbike race, I was not hoping for too much, but I would have still liked to see where I would end up.

Quite some familiar faces at the starting line, so I had a few short chats during the  20 km neutralized start. When we turned to the first dirt roads, it got more serious. The pace went up, the terrain as well. Soon it was night and there were a few small groups climbing up to the Telouet pass together.  Some bigger groups came back on the flatter parts, riders got dropped on the climbs. A some moments it was quite a madmen show. I managed to ride in the first group and during the real ascend of the pass I got in front with one Morrocon rider, just behind the leader. All you could see from time to time were the lights of another rider in front or behind you. On top of the pass it got more and more difficult to cycle, with snow passages and I dipped my feet unwillingly in a pond of icy water.  

When we reached the top, the road suddenly ended and the terrain for real mountainbikers started (which I am not). The mule track led back down to the valley and to the first CP. I was at the top with two other riders and we had difficulties to find the track at the first place. Once we did, the huge stones made it impossible for me to ride. It was a quite long hike-a-bike, while being overtaken by the technically more gifted ones. At one moment Robin and his mate Lukas passed on rigid fork gravel bikes like it was nothing, while I was struggling to just walk the thing.

A bit further I made a small misstep and I slid into a little gutter, expending laterally from the path. It was a wash-out from the recent snowfall and rain. I fell in with my bike on top of me and got really... stuck. It took me a while to figure out how to get out of my situation and after only 5 minutes I managed to push the heavy bike out, followed by dragging my own body out of the ditch. Not of to a good start. 

The rest of the descent was still a struggle with another small crash, so I reached CP1 around place 5-10 in not such a good mood. Having to compensate the lack of technical mountainbike skills with a faster ride would be the red wire throughout this race, even though a race like this is a quite good crash-course. Soon I was doing and daring things I never thought about doing before.

At the CP I filled a ready-meal with hot water and carried under my jersey for half an hour. It was really cold already and the heat of the water also heated up my body. Later I ate my penne bolognaise along the roadside. Little did I know this would be the last decent meal in a long time.

Now that I was completely alone, I could start setting my own pace. Soon there were many single track gravel roads through little villages and long sections of open road going up and down in the middle of nowhere. It was really just you and your bicycle. Many times the path followed the river bed, which meant many rocks and tricky terrain.

After 180km there was finally some proper asphalt road the roadie in me was happy with, but then soon there were more single tracks in villages and endless gravel sections. At first light I reached Toundoute and from there another remote section to Imassine started. I did not have any resupply until then I was starting to get some issues. The section consisted out of a vague path and more then I wanted I ended up in a river bed next to the real path, trying to find the correct track. The end of the section was a straight rolling gravel road after which I reached the 24h gas station on the resupply after 260km.

I loaded up and ate well, ready for the longest remote section of the race (95km without anything). First there was the river crossing at Ait Imlil. I did not bother taking of my shoes. The day would be long and my feet would get dry. The water was surprisingly cold. Soon I started to see more riders (like Sofiane and Anatole) and we were jumping over each other continuously. The first part of this section was quite fast, but you just had to keep on paying attention for the sudden ditches in the terrain. The middle part was one really steep and difficult climb, where I in fact walked more than I rode. Given the steepness, the weight of my bike and my energy state, that was probably the best decision. Given the fact that I stayed at the same position as the riders around me, tells me that was a right decision. 

When the crest was finally reached a really long and fast descent started towards Afra. It was endless and dangerous at some points. I was really hoping my brake pads would not wear away too fast in this very aggressive terrain. Towards the end of the descent, the path became more sandy, which made it tricky to ride sometimes. 

In the late afternoon I reached Afra for a resupply. I arrive right when Anatone left. Soon after me Kevin and Driksen arrived. I was feeling a little under the weather and the food I got did not really stay in that well.  I wasted some time, but I felt sick. When I finally continued going, it was with the intention to find a good place to sleep as soon as it got dark and try to get over the difficult moment. 

The section after Afra is quite sandy and technical but it gets better and faster after a while. I tried to see if some of the cabins in the field would be a good sleeping place, but at the end I settled for a sandy patch under an overhanging rock. Got my bivvy out and slept surrounded by mosquitos for 2.5 hours, right next to the path.

column5: Flanellen benen
Building up slowly again

With dragging brakes and deflated tires. First good ride after TCR. Getting back at it.

'If Brno does not come to me, I will come to Brno'.

Because my hotel in Koceali was a few kilometer West of my original course, I did not want to retrace my steps. So I updated my route slightly and went up the crest over another route than originally planned. This road was a bit longer than the original one, but more importantly it was less steep. It was still challenging, but I am happy I took that option. 

I took my time, as the gaps were still very big. Abdullah was already a while on the finish parcours and Andre was not even in Koceali. Once on the top, the road went up and down a bit, but overall it was quite fine. I took a gravel shortcut of which I am very proud and arrived at the coast line where the finish parcours started.

The finish parcours consisted initially out of consecutive steep climbs up and down. Often the downhill was full of potholes, so taking advantage of the descending speed was not easy. Just before dawn I had a little dip, so I ate a bit and had a 15 minutes powernap while sitting on a terrace chair of a restaurant, with a view on the dark coast line. When I continued, I noticed Abdullah did not make that much progress yet, which surprised me. But I did not think anything more of it yet.

I would have liked to have some resupplies, but all the shops were still closed. A bit frustrating, but I had to push on. The next part was a gravel road hugging the coast going up and down. Very beautiful, but a hard.

At the end of the gravel section I finally found an open shop and got a final resupply. Abdullah still seemed to be stuck, so I started to think there might be something wrong or there might be opportunities. I would keep on pushing - a bit harder now - and get to the top of the hills first and then reassess.

The climbs went quite smoothly. On the top I saw Abdullah was not very far ahead and with potential time penalties, there might still have been a chance to claim a podiul spot. I decided to go all in to the finish line, give it all I got until the finish line. 

Sadly my powermeter did not work that day, but my speeds in Istanbul were consistently well over 30kph. I felt superstrong and only stopped for traffic lights. The kilometers to the finish went down, but I kept to my plan and pushed until the end. Maybe at one point I would see Abdullah in front of me. It would be a miracle, given the gap a few hours ago, but he seemed to be slowly dying and going very slow. 

5km from the finish, 4km, 3km,... no one in sight. I almost thought about taking it slower, but I remember the promise I made a pushed on till the end.

The parcours followed the bicycle path at the waterfront at the Bosporus. It turns left and right the whole time, so you cannot see far ahead. After another turn in a little park, some 500 meter before the finish line, I suddenly saw a cyclist with an Apidura saddle bag in front of me. Is that him? It must be him! He was going at a snail pace and I geared up once again, accelerated once again and sprinted passed him. My gps indicated 450m before the finish. This must be a millimeter sprint in terms of ultracycling. 

I sprinted to the stairs leading up to the finish, got off my bike and pushed it up as fast as possible the 25 steps. A 100 meter later I reached the finish and claimed the 3rd place in disbelief. For the second year in a row, for the second time in a special way. But this 3rd place tasted so much sweeter. I am so proud.

After some strange finish interviews and pictures I enjoyed my first beer in years. Quite a while later Abdullah arrived at the finish line. Apparently, he also still made a navigational mistake in the last kilometers and he had to correct this and follow the official parcours correctly. That took a while in his state, but even if he would have followed the correct trajectory, I would have flewn passed him. I feel a bit sorry for him, being in the top 3 all of the race, but the finsh line counts in sport. 

After a great result, with a 3rd place overall and a victory in the Green Leaderboard, I will now have some well-deserved rest and enjoy some time in Istanbul. Thanks for following!

When I woke up after 3 hours in Biga, Abdullah was already far away. None of my chasers made it this far neither. So it looked like it was all going to be about defending the gap and making sure I at least finished 4th.

The route followed bigger roads and flatter plains and was therefor quite easy until the city with the fancy name Mustafakemalpasa - named after Atatürk. There I found some good bread in a bakery and I continued up the hills with olive plantages. 

It was quite challenging rough asphalt and a lot of climbing. Not a lot of civilization. When I was approaching the top, I saw that my gps had nearly no battery left and when I wanted to charge it, I discovered my powerbank was out of juice as well.

In panic I tried to charge it with my phone battery, but then I could of course not use it anymore for navigating. Then I remember the built-in feature I have on my bike, which I barely use. But it is there for these situations. I can charge my powerbank while riding, using my dynamo. A little more riding resistance, but it will take me home. Stupid me... why didn't I just charge my powerbank in the hotel last night?

Closer to the top there were some quarries and a lot of dust and trucks on the road. I arrived to Kayapa, where some guys where interested in what I was doing. I had a chat with them while I was having my first soup in ages. 

The big city of Bursa was the next hurdle on the way. Bursa is the 4th city of Turkey and I had to transverse it completely from West to East, so that would not be the nicest ride. Roads where busy and the temperatures went up and I was relieved when I made it to the road towards Yenisehir.

Here my worst moments of the day however started. First you needed to climb out of Bursa on a steep climb next to busy traffic. Then there was a strong headwind which made progress hard. In the only village I passed through I had a liter of ice tea and tried to sit down or have a powernap. The guy of the shop however kept me bothered and I felt tired and in a bad mood.

I went on a bit further to Yenisehir, in desperate need of a boost or a break. Just behind the city I found a gas station where I wanted to buy some supplies. The girl in the gas station wanted to give me again a plastic bag for all the stuff (I have been offered 100s of plastic bags in Turkey, what would I do with that?) and then she wanted to use her phone to explain me something, whereas I just wanted to pay my goods, eat them and sit down. It suddenly got the most of me. Just take my card and I pay, I am too tired for chitchat. Frustrated I left the station and sat down on the ground for 5 minutes. When I went back, she had her text ready, saying it was 70 lira. Very nice of her, but at that moment I could not care less, so I paid by card, took my things and tried to have a powernap.

I gathered all my courage for the next part. I knew it would be extremely hard. In the midday sun I had to do a 5 kilometer 8% climb or so, next to a busy road and with a headwind. I just got into a small gear and went for it. The meters counted down slowly, but I was so relieved when I reached the top.

The downhill was very fast. Because of the hard wind I had even difficulties to stay on the bike.  I had a celebratory ice cream in the next gas station when I got down. A lot of stopping and struggling this day, but it was the only way to keep going.

The lake of Iznit was very beautiful and it was a wonderful change to pass once through a historical city. After Iznit I had to do another climb, away from the lake and back to sea level   at Koceali. The climb started very steep and was pretty long. Towards the end it kept on going up and down for a while, until I could descent into Gölcük. 

Checking the tracker taught me that I had time to have a sit-down meal and that I would better still sleep another night, seeing the progress the top 3 had only made. I had chicken wings with Turkish sparkling water (aka limonade) and did my final stretch of the day to Koceali. It is a busy city and I took a while to find my hotel. Check-in went surprisingly fast. The hotel room was however clearly a smoking room, so I had to sleep with the windows open in order to survive. I decided to sleep more than 3 hours this time, as it would not change anything to the final positions anymore anyway.

column3: TCR10 - day 8b: The woods of hell
column5:
I woke up when the last trucks were about to leave the ferry and jumped up. I did not wake David. He would manage by himself, and besides, it was an unsupported race. With the wind in the back I then flew the 30 kilometers from Lapseki to Canakkale. David was nowhere to be seen anymore. He would at the end stay a while at the CP to recover.

The crew at CP4 was really friendly and I managed to secure some ice cubes from the hotel restaurant. I was very worried about the coming parcours, knowing how warm it gets and and with the expected headwind. I wanted to be well-prepared and have enough water with me. I got some more ice at a ice-coffee bar and got some final supplies at a gas station. They even sold sushi there. Not bad for a potential last meal :-p .

The road up to the start of the parcours was already dreadful and endless. Very steep, but luckily still in asphalt. There were many water fountains for cattle, but I did not trust you could drink it safely, so I rationed my own water. I could however still use it to make my sleeves and cap wet and to cool down.

Once on the parcours I pushed on, even if it went slow. On one of the longer steep climbs the heat caught up with me. I told to myself I would rest as soon as I saw a cattle drinking tank. When one finally showed up at the left side, it was greenish or blueish and it did not look that healthy, but I just soaked my arms in it, found some shadow under a thorn tree, tried to eat something and put my alarm for 15 min later. 

Both the eating and the napping where not really successful, but it was just enough to gather my strength and continue pushing up the hill. Or course a bit further superior resting places and cattle tanks could be found, with one of them even having sofas standing next to it, but I already had my rest.

The struggle and rationing continued, but after many more off road kilometers and one nearly-crash, I finally reached the end of the parcours in the village of Balcilar. I was happy, but knew this ordeal was not over yet. I still needed food and drinks urgently and I knew that the first shop was only a 23km and 300 height meter further. So I had to keep on slowly progressing.

It was around 8-9pm when I reach heaven. 'Halleluja' and 'Gloria' I proclaimed to the surprised shop owner when I took a big liter bottle of cola out of the fridge. I stayed quite a while and had many more supplies. The guy even spoke some English, so I explained him that the coming days his shop would be the light at the end of the tunnel of many people.

I continued a bit further to the bigger city of Biga, where I found many mosquitos and a much needed hotel. There was quite a gap between me and my chasers and apparently the number 3 in the race, Abdullah, was still sleeping here when I arrived. I decided to put my alarm 2 hours and 40 minutes later.

At night the traffic in Alexandroupolis was a lot less. It is a big party city apparently, as it was still very vivid when I arrived. I had to get into Turkey today and hopefully finish the last parcours. 

The wind was strong and had turned in North-Eastern direction. This made it, even at night, more challenging to reach the border crossing.

When approaching the Ipsala border crossing point, I saw kilometers of cars queueing on the highway before the border crossing. I imagined already issues showing up ahead of me. Undisturbed I tried to get as close as possible to the checking gates and I 'cut' the queue just at the end... sorry! But I am in a race and I have only a bike...

The Turkish German I cut in front of understandingly did not agree with my methods and got out to hand over his family's passports to the officer before I could hand over mine. I got one place back, got also my picture taken and could skip the second check, because I was not by car. I left to the Turkey side well ahead of the angry driver. The Turkish side logically a lot faster, but in total I still spend half an hour crossing from the EU into Turkey.

The first 30 kilometers where on a flagged, but allowed road but went by pretty fast. After that stretch you then had to turn off-road right before Kesan, which meant navigating multiple groups of dogs. Welcome to Turkey! I guess I walked more in this section then I rode. I was really happy to reach the proper town, but then the dog adventures were not over yet.

My route to avoid to forbidden main road going down brought me a little back West and followed mainly asphalt roads. There was a lot of climbing and it got so humid that my gps started to act weird. I was relieved to reach lower ground again, even if that meant a lot of gravel. 

A bit later my route joined the only possible road crossing the peninsula and right there I met David, who was just a few minutes after me at CP3. For some reason, the hunderds of kilometers in Greece or Bulgaria at the end led to a very similar overall needed time. 

As the amount of route options here was very limited, I was then also very surprised when he suddenly turned to the main road, even if that was prohibited. I saw my chance and pushed on hard over the gravel roads towards Gelibolu to take the ferry to the Asian side. I arrived 5 minutes before ferry departure and saw that David was still a few kilometers away. However, Turkish ferry boats are not very punctual and even if he was 10 min late, he made it to the boat. A missed opportunity to gain a 30 minutes lead like that.

I had parked my bike at the front of the boat, to be out quickly and went to the little cafe on the boat to buy ice cream, crisps and drinks. David came there as well, but he seemed very tired and had difficulties to just strike a conversation. At the end we both laid down and fell asleep.

At night I crossed the border to Greece for a day of Greek fun. I knew that resupplying would be hard, especially the first half. It all went quite smoothly however for the first hours. If had to do some little detours and a short powernap, but I reached Serres in time for a quite large breakfast.

On the road to the coastal town Kavala it got warmer and hillier. Also the Greek 'flat' was not really corporative. A bit before noon I reached Kavala, hoping for a good lunch. Having passed all good possibilities apparently, I had to settle for a tavern that sold the same sugary crap as they sell in all gas stations. I got quite grumpy.

There was more and more headwind towards Xanthi and the temperatures shot up. I found some good and quick lunch along the way at the end, but not long after the wind, temperatures and sad environment made it a struggle to continue.

In Komotini, I had a quite long supermarket break and decided to push on to Nea Chili, right before Alexandroupolis, where I had booked a room. The lady was very friendly, understanding and helpful. After I checked in, I could still order a Greek kebab and went to sleep.

Tutin still allowed to fetch some supplies in the evening, before setting off to Montenegro. At some traffic light for road works I got bothered by the worker's dogs. With my Western European mind it is hard to comprehend why they are not chained up or closed up if this obviously will happen. A honking car and a worker who suddenly got out made it possible for me to continue and get to the border of Montenegro. After that, the road with tunnels and bridges brought me to the long, but not so hard climb to the Kosovo border. I still found a very busy and open gas station before Rozaje.

At the top of the climb, there was a border police agent sitting completely alone in the middle of the night and in the middle of the forest. He just looked at my ID card quickly and that was it... good night.

The descent was very long a cold with many hairpin turns. The amount of stray dogs in Kosovo was a lot lower than what I had imagined before. There were a few, but far of the Romania level. 

Kosovo also seemsed to be quite flat in the center and densily populated. With a rear wind I reached the old city of Prizren in the morning and with two peaches in my pockets I started tackling the third parcours. The climb was not very and the scenery was not very special in my opinion.

At the other side of the hill, the CP was in an old authentic house. Very beautiful. I had some local breakfast and stayed some 20 minutes. I passed the CP in 5th position. The next rider David was about to arrive soon after, then there would be a quite big gap.

I wondered if David would soon pass me, but when I did not see him at the top of the climb to North-Macedonia, I figured out he probably took the Bulgaria route. My route took me for the descent over a bad gravel road with thorns at the side. I damaged my shirt, but got down safely for the rest.

At the bottom, there was a narrow road. It felt like someone had switched on the heating. Some local dotwatchers waited for me on the road and I had a short chat with them. The road to Skopje was a lot harder than I hoped and it was also a lot more difficult to resupply. Yes, plenty of gas stations, but none of them gave me what I wanted.

I then followed the cycling path across and through the middle of the little country. In the midday heat I had to come over the hardest part to Veles, which is a steep and curvy gravel climb. After that, the route basically follows old and seemingly abandonned dual carriage roads. You could just cycle in the middle if you wanted, almost nobody used them anymore since the highway was built. The road was basically flat or downhill. Every 25km there was a town to resupply and I stopped for the night in Valandovo.

I had called before, but it was still hard to explain everything. At the end I asked for two pizzas, of which I only managed to eat one. The pizza was quite local, but had - at my specific request - tomatoes this time :-) .

column3: TCR10 - day 5: Bosnian gravel, seemingly wrong choices, cracking bikes and shepherds
column5:
I started still before midnight on the next big endaevour. I finished the last kilometers to Bjelasnica hearing and fearing stray dogs continuously. A fear which was not needed here at the end. They all seemed to be far away or locked up. Bjelasnica is a big winter sport center that hosted the Winter Olympics of Sarajevo in 1984. It is full of big, modern apartments.

The gravel parcours started right outside the city. The steep slopes and loose gravel made it difficult to stay on the bike sometimes. A bit further up, outside of the forest, it flattened out, but the gravel got worse, so you had to hike. I saw some other rider's light and walked past Daniel who was struggling on his 32mm tires. A bit later, there miraculously appeared some asphalt sections, but they were soon followed again by gravel and hike-a-bikes. 

When finally reaching CP2, some riders where sleeping inside (and therefor in theory behind me). I officially passed as 9th, before quickly continuing the long cold descent South. Another big asphalt climb to the pass and a downhill to the village of Odzaci still had to be completed to finalize this official parcours.

This time the fear for dogs was better placed. I had no big issues, but I heard later that Christopher was bitten there a few hours earlier.

At the end of the parcours there was another dilemma. There was the full gravel road to Kalinovik, the full asphalt road detour almost all the way back North to Sarajevo and back, or something in between. After some doubting, I opted for the save and 40km longer asphalt detour, with a lot more climbing. 

When tracing back my steps to the North, I met other cyclists completing the parcours in the other direction and I started to regret my route choice more and more. There was however no turning back. But the good thing was that it still gave me the opportunity to see the beautiful sceneries at the first light of day.

Low on supplies, I reached the end of my detour and a gas station close to Foca in the morning. To my surprise and satisfaction, still well ahead of the group of riders I overtook over the last few days. They were all still struggling on the gravel roads, which, in hindsight, were not that easy or fast. A controversial, but good decision at the end.

From Foca there were plenty of routing options to the next CP in Kosovo. I knew the option straight through Montengro would be nice, but full of gravel. The less straight forward option going past Gorazde and then to Rudo and Serbia would be longer, but flatter and better. 

The way there felt a bit as a struggle, especially when something in my bike started to crack like mad with every pedal stroke. I had had it in Germany before and solved it then with squirting some chain oil in the water evacuation hole at my bottom bracket. This time this did not work. For some hours I cycled with enormously irritation noice and my mind was more occupied with getting rid or it then with the race. At the end - and as a last resort - I took my chain lube again and sprayed it everywhere around my bracket, chainrings, cassette and cranks. At first this did not seem to work again. But after a few pedal strokes the cracking noise silenced with every other revolution...until it died out. Finally rest again.

I could focus on the race now and got ready in the midday heat for the long climb to Nova Varoŝ. I knew that road from TCR8. It was again way too busy and dangerous. I stopped in a supermarket for a resupply. After Nova Varoš I had to climb even a long time further to reach the plateau at Sjenica. It was clearly a poorer area and there was no data connection that allowed my to look for accommodations in advance.

After Sjenica, there was a surprisingly interesting area where shepherds take care of there herds on a flatter plain in the highlands. It felt like a different world. Wonderful experience. I decided not to try to reach Montenegro or Kosovo still tonight, but that I would find a place in Tutin after the descent.

Good thing the word 'hotel' is quite international, as almost nobody in Tutin spoke English. Some speak some German and it is clear that many people live or have lived in Germany before.

Using google translate I explained my situation to the receptionist of the 'most expensive hotel' in Tutin and after some difficulties to understand it from his side, I got a room for 30 euro. Even though the city outside was very busy with all bars and restaurants full, it was hard for me to find still a quick evening bite. When returning to the hotel, the friendly receptionist however still managed to arrange a pizza margarita (only dough and cheese, tomatoes are alien here) in less than 10 minutes. I had the impression he had ordered delivery food before :-) . I ate it all and got rested.

After Zagreb I came on familiar grounds. I took this same route along Velika Gorica in TCR last year. This time I passed earlier on the day (during the night in fact), so it was a lot calmer. In contrast to last year, I did not take the hilly road straight to Banja Luka then, but the slightly longer and more popular detour over the North. The road from Sisak was very long and straight, with family houses and farms at both sides of the route. It was a very annoying road, so I was really happy when I reached the Bosnian border. 

In Bosnia, I visit the accomodations of the first gas station and a bit later I had to take a power nap on a bench, to counteract some upcoming fatigue. I checked the tracking once and saw I made almost connection with a row of good cyclists, all heading to Banja Luka. I took some surprisingly lovely country roads and the main road later became quite busy when approaching the city. 

The bakery in the city sold me burek and bread and I fully resupplied for the next hard section. I did the same section last year and now it was again superwarm and hard. I spend most of the day reaching Knezevo and then Turbe, after going up and down for ages on bad roads.

Down in the valley, we were not allowed to use the now banned main road to Vitez, but we had to find an alternative. For me that meant following the old rail road that used to be there. It is in fact a bad gravel road which goes everywhere. Hike-a-bike was often a necessity.

In Travnik I plundered a small shop and cleaned my mussette from the molten chocolate that got smeared everywhere in it. I did not use it anymore for a while. At this moment in the race, yoghurt and milk products were my favourite. Not recommended by dietitians, but what do they know about ultracycling anyway?

The path followed through the remarkably beautiful city center and after a few steep and gravel sections, I reaches the allowed part of the main road. It was however still very busy and dangerous.

I sat down for a while in a gas station bar to escape the heat and to decide on my future steps. I was doubting between sleeping before or on the Bosnian parcours. After changing my mind a few times, I kept my booking on the long climb to Bjelasnica. A good decision at the end. Even if it was still early and light outside, I could use the rest before the parcours, which I would have to do in darkness anyway, waiting or not.

The mountain hut at the side of the street, a few kilometers from the old Olympic city looked abandonned. But one guy had stayed to give me the key, explain me where to put it when I left and to provide me with a Bosnian 'dinner'. Some fried dough with a cheese dip and bacon strips. He left the whole place to me alone, I ate my dinner and when to bed.

column3: TCR10 - day 3: Steep, steeper, steepest, steepestest,... and then flat
column5:
After a good 2.5 hours of sleep, I woke up a little after midnight to tackle the first beast of the day: the Katschberg. Before the race I had never even heard about this climb, but it is a real animal. Only 5 kilometers, but more than double digits on average. It is really crawling up on endless slopes up to 18-20%. It took ages, but I was so happy it was over. I knew that, if I could overcome this obstacle, the rest should be possible as well.

I climbed up using my less bright battery lights, as my dynamo light uses some Watts, which I really wanted to keep for climbing up. When I wanted to change to dynamo light on the top however, that one did not seem to work anymore. Or ar least not as it should have. After faffing around a bit in the cold and swaping and taking out connectors, it functioned again. Time lost, but no race yet.

I rode down towards Gmünd and Spittal and followed the Drau river to Villach. A little detour, but a flat one at least, as the other option would have been to go more directly South and climb a lot more. I found an open gas station at night in Villach center and did a full stock up to continue to the next hurdles. 

Climbing up over Italy to the Predel Pass and Slovenia, I passed some known grounds, as I already was there in TCR8 and in the TUR earlier this year. After the border crossing, the first parcours of this edition started. The climb up to Mangart was 10 kilometer long at 10%. I started off on economy and soon it started to rain. Because you had to go up and down the same climb, it was interesting to see other riders descending or going up. So you can estimate the time you are ahead or behind. 

At the top it was raining a lot, so I sadly could not enjoy the amazing views. My gps also acted up because of the rain. Some frustrations, but soon I was back on the way down. The parcours is in one of the most beautiful areas I know, passing the blue Soca river and then going up the Vrsic Pass where the first check point was. A long steep climb again and I was glad it was over. The last kilometers were a real struggle. 

I reached the CP as 9th and 1st on the green leaderboard. I spoke to some French followers and fixed the dynamo issue more permanent. The restaurant in the mountain hut did not open for another 15 minutes and I did not want to wait for that. So I decided to ride down with an empty stomach and try my luck in the valley. I followed the great cycling paths in Slovenia. It took a while, but I found an amazing restaurant in Jesenik which could provide a fantastic and big lunch immediately. I enjoyed it for the full 100%.

Riding through Slovenia is amazing and easy. Good roads, friendly people and lots of resupplies. I had a good route and soon I got close to the Croatian border. After eating a kebab, I continued to my hotel close to Lucko, under Zagreb. A bit an expensive hotel, but the least of my worries.

Most ultracyclists go to sleep after midnight, preferring some darkness before and after their sleep. Other ride till very late and get up when it gets light. I am one of the only ones probably who does the opposite: I go to sleep around dusk. There are many reasons for this. It makes it for instance easier to still find a suitable sleeping spot or to check into a hotel for the night. At the same time it give me the opportunity to see what the competition did at night before they went to sleep. You are kind of a sleeping cycle ahead. Not that I check the race status often in the beginning of the race (it brings more stress than anything else), but towards the end it can become an advantage.

So, of we go... day 2. I soon reached the area around Stuttgart. Many short sharp climbs. Surprisingly I found an open gas station, so I could resupply for my route through Germany. It was a frustrating night, with closed roads due to road works and closed roads due to whatever other reason. Wir arbeiten für Sie! You work against me now... So I had to improvise quite some detours.

In the morning I reached Augsburg where there was even a TCR fan standing along the street :-). On typical German rural main roads I rode on to Dachau, where the traffic light challenge of Munich started. During planning I knew that was an issue when going though the city, but I decided the advantage of shorter distance, less hills and plenty of resupply possibilities would outweigh that disadvantage. With my musette and shirt full or resupplies from Lidl (mmm... drinking yoghurt) I continued.

After Munich, (too) big roads brought me to the Traunsee. Beautiful, but busy. Some calmer roads then led me to a small cyclist bridge crossing into Austria. Now the real work could start.

I stopped at a Spar supermarket I knew in Hallein and had to wait (too long) for them to prepare me two sandwiches with ham and mustard to take in the Alps. The long wait meant that my short lead over Ben and Pavel (which I just met and overtook before) would have been completely gone. I felt bad about it, even if it was still so early in the race. Nevertheless I wanted to rectify it as soon as possible. 

Soon I overtook Ben again on a climb and left him behind. After Radstadt, the first big challenge of this TCR followed: the Obertauern Pass. 15km at 7%, but a lot steeper in the beginning. I had forgotten how it felt. The kilometers passed by slowly and I was really happy to reach the top. 

I had hoped the descent would have been a fast one, but soon it seemed not. I had to keep peddling all the way down. I was getting cold, despite my extra thermal layer. It was already dark when I reached the accommodation I booked competely on the bike a few hours before). That was enough for the day. For sure if you knew how I had to start day 3. When packing out, I still met the media crew. The asked my questions while being busy and tired, so I have no idea (yet) how the end result sounded.

column3: TCR10 - day 1: The Race is on!
column5:
I write all these short reports when I am at the finish location in Istanbul (spoiler!), so it has been a while since I did these rides. I will however try to provide a summary according to the best of my memories, as long as those are not impacted by sleep deprivation :-).

The race started this year in Roubaix, famous as the finish location the well-known Paris-Roubaix classics. The velodrome was the decor for start parade, followed by a neutralized start of about 15km. 

Luckily the starting parcours did not take on the Roubaix cobbles, but rather the Flanders cobbles and hills. Still very challenging of course. Kluisberg, Oude Kwaremont, Paterberg, Kopoenberg, Taaienberg, Muur,... all with a fully loaded bike in the first 70k. But I loved it. These were the roads where I grew up as a cyclist and I was among the first 10 riders constantly. Especially on the Muur it was great. Despite not having the start of the race this year, the atmosphere in the last 100s meters was amazing. Music, commentators,... I fully joined in and cheered for the public.

And then... there was silence. That is always a bit strange in TCR. As soon as you reach the end of the start parcours, everybody goes their own route and you are alone.

I took the more boring route straight through Brussels and following the infamous Flemish steenwegen. Some others opted for the ride through the Ardennes, but that was of course more hilly, despite being some 20k shorter. I assumed that I would still have to climb enough later in the race, so better to save those climbing legs a bit now. 

Brussels went surprising smooth, besides the always present traffic lights. After that I passed Leuven, Tienen and Tongeren on my way to Maastricht. It is surprising and concerning to see how easy it is to find and buy fuel and bread (and even fruit) at night in Flanders, but there is no place where you can just get drinking water...

After the little hills in the Netherlands and Germany I reached the Rhine river the next morning. The Rhine cycling paths are a cycling highway, but sometimes you still have a lot of traffic lights were you still lose time and the German bicycle path inside the cities are always a disaster, as you can never really count on them.

After the Rhine, I crossed over the wine hills to Mannheim, where I finally crossed the Rhine on my way towards Stuttgart. After about 24 hours of cycling, I felt it was enough and I checked in in a little hotel an hour or so before the big city. First day finished, was pretty efficient and made good progress (even if other still got a lot further). Surprsingly I just met maybe 2 or 3 other riders during the whole day, so that meant I must be doing well, as the positions are distributed more sparsely towards the head of the race.

My turn to be proud once and post a victory ride :-). Preparation race for TCR, but it went pretty well with lead from the first meter until the finish.

Very beautiful, but very hard race with many challenging gravel sections. Like a connection of 20 TCR parcours. A great idea to reduce some tire pressure. 

Planned to sleep for 1.5 hours at Rest Point 3 at 840km, but I overslept and slept for 3 hours at the end. No worries, the lead was still there and accounted to 8 hours at the finish line.

Thanks to Radomir and the supporting team. Great race and ride to discover the Czech Republic.

Now rest, stretch, eat and drink and get physically and mentally ready for in two weeks.
Almost there...

column3: TCR09 - Day 8 - The death of the hero
column5: Shot off to Ioannina, made sure to resupply sufficiently for the horror to come. After two monster climbs I finally reached the 4a parcours. At the end the doubt started: around or over the hill? I made the wrong choice to go around, got stuck in the deadly Greek afternoon sun, while everything was closed. When I finally found an open restaurant I had to rest a while and resupply. But I was still in the race!

The 50km stretch to the 3rd parcours As already that bad, that there was not even a need for a parcours at all anymore. Potholes and gravel everywhere. But the parcours still had to come: the worst gravel roads imaginable with an old cobble stone road with half of the cobbles missing and the gaps filled with stones the size of eggs. After a stressful descent the roads got a bit better in North-Macedonia and the first part of Southern Albania, to end with long stretches of gravel towards the Greek border. As the border was closed at night, I had to sleep a bit longer than anticipated.
Enjoying the scenery in Bosnia and especially Montenegro. A quick bike check in Niksic and then crossing the planes to Albania. Getting ready for the hard parts.
